theme: Peace with God; Adam and Christ
readingInstruction: Read Romans 5:1-21. The chapter moves from the benefits of justification to the way sin and grace work in history through two men, Adam and Christ. Read verses 1-11 for the experience of salvation, and 12-21 for the structure of salvation history.
settingTheScene: Chapters 1 to 4 have shown that we are justified by faith. Chapter 5 begins with the word “Therefore.” What follows from justification? First, peace, access, and hope. Then Paul steps back and places the whole human story in two heads: Adam, in whom all die, and Christ, in whom all who believe are made alive. This is a pivotal chapter for understanding how the covenants fit together.
observation: “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (5:1).
“And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (5:5).
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (5:8).
“For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (5:10).
“Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (5:12).
“Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come” (5:14).
“For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (5:19).
“But where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20).
interpretation:
“Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God.” This is peace as a status, an end to hostility. We were enemies, and now we are at peace. We have access by faith into the grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. Paul even says we rejoice in our sufferings, because suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope. And hope does not disappoint us because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Notice that all three persons of the Trinity are active: peace with God the Father through the Son, and the Spirit pouring love into our hearts.

The proof of God’s love is the cross. “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” We were weak, ungodly, sinners, and enemies. Few would die for a righteous man, though perhaps for a good man someone would dare. But Christ died for the ungodly. And Paul reasons from the greater to the lesser: if God did the hard thing while we were enemies, he will do the easy thing now that we are reconciled. We will be saved from the wrath through him. We rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

Then comes the great comparison, from verse 12. Sin entered the world through one man, Adam, and death through sin, so death spread to all because all sinned. This does not simply mean that Adam set a bad example. Adam acted as the head of the human race, and what he did had consequences for all who were in him. Christians have explained the details differently: some hold that Adam’s guilt is directly counted to us (the federal headship view), others that we inherit a corrupt nature and then sin ourselves. All agree that sin and death came through Adam and cannot be escaped by our own efforts. Paul calls Adam “a type of the one who was to come.”

Christ is the second Adam. The parallel is not exact: the free gift is not like the trespass. If many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. As one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life. The point is stated plainly: “as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.”

Where did the law fit in? It came in to increase the trespass, to show the true nature of sin, “but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Grace wins. Grace is stronger than sin.
connection: Genesis 2 to 3 is the account of Adam and the fall. 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and 15:45-49 contrast Adam and Christ. Luke 3:38 and Luke 4 show Jesus as the second Adam, tested in the wilderness. Hebrews 2:5-18 speaks of Christ as the true Man. Colossians 1:19-22 speaks of reconciliation. 2 Corinthians 5:18-21 is the ministry of reconciliation. Ephesians 2:1-10 describes our being made alive. Isaiah 53:11 says the righteous one will make many to be accounted righteous. 1 John 4:10 says love consists in that he loved us and sent his Son.
application:
Count your suffering as a means God uses to build hope. Is there an area where you can see this?

Meditate on Romans 5:8 today. Let it silence your doubts about God’s love.

Thank Jesus for being the second Adam, who obeyed where Adam failed.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for peace with him through Jesus.
Thank him for pouring his love into your heart by the Spirit.
Thank him for loving you while you were a sinner.
